To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the periodicity of a kink in TM4, the signature residues in the TM2-3, TM8-9, and flanking TMSs, and the accessibility of Arg-126 to the extracellular solution are critical for GLUT1 function.

mutations of GLUT1 in patients with GLUT1 deficiency syndrome are concentrated in TM4, which is the catalytic core for all MFS transporters, and that Arg-126 is the most frequently mutated amino acid in GLUT1, which is located at the amino-terminal end of TM4 and is a key residue in the structure of the MFS transporters.
mutations in the MFS transporter GLUT1 that cause GLUT1 Deficiency Syndrome (GLUT1DS) are clustered in TM4, a helix that is exposed to the extracellular solution.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the structure-function relationship of GLUT1, a glucose transporter that is critical for the normal functioning of the brain and the retina.

understanding the molecular basis of a human encephalo- myopathy that results from defective glucose flux through the brain endothelium and with the molecular mechanisms by which MFS proteins transport solutes across membranes.
the structure and mechanism of the human glucose transporter, GLUT1, a member of the major facilitator superfamily of transporters.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the GLUT1 transporter is a member of the MFS superfamily and that the structural features that distinguish the GLUT1 transporter from other members of this superfamily include the presence of a helical TM4 and the absence of a helical loop between TMs 5 and 6.
the MFS transporter GLUT1 has a kinked helical structure that is stabilized by a conserved pattern of charges, and the kink is located at TM4, the site for the most common GLUT1 mutations.
the MFS TM4 is a helix that is kinked at a conserved arginine, and the helix is exposed at the transporter surface where it is accessible to a proton.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the structural signatures in GLUT1 are critical for the protein's structure and function.
mutations that cause GLUT-1 deficiency syndrome are located at the MFS signature sequences, the glycines, and TM4, where the helix kinks and surfaces into the extracellar solution.
the MFS signature loops and TM4 helix are the structural signatures of the GLUT1 transporter and that mutations that affect these structures result in GLUT1 deficiency syndrome.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a single residue in TM4 of a MFS transporter, GLUT1, can be a target for mutations in a human disease.

the periodicity of a mutant residue in a TM domain can be a clue to its location in a transporter and that mutations that disrupt the structure and function of the transporter are more likely to be associated with disease.
the MFS TM4 is an important structural component in the transport cycle of the GLUTs.
